notes.text: Lesson 7: Arrays. An array is one variable that holds a list of values, in order. MakeArray builds a list from the items wired into it. Each item has a position (its index), and positions start at 0, not 1.

Try it: (1) Step (F11) and watch scores in the Variables panel of the Debugger tab. (2) Add a fifth score with another ArrayAdd. (3) Use ArrayGet#<i32> to print only the first score (index 0). (4) Ask ArrayGet for index 10 and read the error message.
ArrayAdd puts one more item on the end of the array. scores now holds 4 items.
ForEach runs 'each' once for every item. item is the value, index is its position. After the last item it follows 'done'.

notes.text: Lesson 8: Structs and enums. An enum is a short list of named choices: a Mood is Happy, Hungry or Sleepy, and nothing else. A struct bundles several values into one: a Pet has a name and a mood. Both are declared at the top of the Source pane.

Try it: (1) Step (F11) into Show and look at p in the Variables panel. (2) Right-click the value pin of 'hungry' and set it to Mood.Sleepy. (3) In the Source pane, add a field 'age: i32 = 1' to Pet and watch 'Make Pet' grow a pin. (4) Right-click an output pin that carries a Pet and choose 'Break into fields'.
Make Pet builds a Pet from its fields. mood is not wired, so it takes its default, Mood.Happy.
WithField makes a copy of the pet with one field changed. Structs never change in place, so the copy is stored back in pet.

notes.text: Lesson 9: Maps. A map stores a value under each key, like a dictionary: here, how many times each fruit appears. MapFind looks a key up (a missing key gives 0), and MapSet stores a new value under it. A map remembers the order keys were first added.

Try it: (1) Add a fifth fruit to the array (right-click 'fruits', more inputs) and run again. (2) Step (F11) through the first loop and watch counts grow in the Variables panel. (3) Change the key type: what has to change with it?
A key that is not there yet gives 0, so the first apple counts as 0 + 1.
ForEachMap visits every key in the order it was first added, with its value.

notes.text: Lesson 10: Errors. Dividing by zero has no answer, so it is an error, and normally an error stops the whole program. A Try node catches it instead: what is wired after 'body' runs protected, and if something in it goes wrong, 'fault' runs with the error's message. Either way, 'then' runs afterwards.

Try it: (1) Change 0 in 'zero' to 2: now 'never' prints, and 'fault' is skipped. (2) Disconnect 'sorted.fault' and run: the age error now stops the program, and the error panel names the node. (3) Make your own Throw with your own message.
Everything wired after 'body' is protected by this Try.

notes.text: Lesson 11: Waiting. An event can pause partway and carry on later: Delay waits a number of seconds of game time. Main is an event here, not a func, because it waits. While one event waits, a game keeps running everything else.

Try it: (1) Change the wait to 0.5 and run: the countdown takes half as long in game time (see the time printed in the Output). (2) Count down from 5. (3) Try putting a Delay in a func: Wiret asks you to mark it @latent, because whatever calls it will have to wait too.
The event stops here for one second, then the loop carries on where it was.

notes.text: Lesson 12: Objects. A class describes a kind of thing: its fields (what each one knows) and its methods (what each one can do). New makes an object of a class. Dog and Cat extend Animal, so they are Animals too, and can each speak in their own way.

Try it: (1) Step (F11) into Speak and look at self in the Variables panel. (2) Give Animal a second field, 'legs: i32 = 4', and use it in Speak. (3) Delete Cat's Speak: Tom now speaks like any animal.
Each pet runs its own class's Speak, though the array only knows they are Animals.

notes.text: Lesson 13: Interfaces. An interface is a promise: any class that says 'impl Shape' has an Area and a Name. Rectangle and Triangle are not related, but both keep the promise, so one array can hold both and ask each for its area.
Try it: (1) Add a Circle class that implements Shape (the Source pane is easiest). (2) Remove Name from Triangle: Wiret says which method the promise is missing. (3) Make the square's sides 6.
Calling through the interface: each shape's own class decides what runs.

notes.text: Lesson 14: Events. A dispatcher is a list of listeners on an object: Bind adds one, Unbind removes one, and Broadcast calls them all. A listener is a delegate, made with CreateDelegate from a function, or from a method plus the object to call it on.

Try it: (1) Move the Unbind to the end: Announce hears all three clicks. (2) Make a second Counter and bind it too. (3) Change Heard to an event with a Delay: a delegate starts an event on its own, so Click does not wait.
After this, Announce stops listening, but the counter goes on.
